How to Buy IP Legal Services: What You Need and What You Don’t

One of the more frustrating parts of being an international business lawyer is watching companies spend thousands of dollars protecting intellectual property that presents little risk while leaving their most valuable assets exposed. We see companies pay for confidentiality agreements they do not need, register trademarks in the wrong countries or classes, and develop products without making sure they will own the resulting designs and tooling.

Then their manufacturer starts selling their products to competitors, refuses to return their molds, or a distributor registers their trademark. Fixing these problems costs far more than preventing them, and sometimes there is no good solution.

The problem usually starts before the lawyers get involved. Business owners decide they need a trademark, patent, NDA, or IP agreement without first figuring out what they are trying to prevent. They then shop for the lowest price and tell their lawyer exactly what they need, and their lawyer gives that to them.

The lawyers at my law firm (and many other law firms) start by trying to identify what would hurt the business if someone copied it, took it, or prevented the company from using it. Once you understand those risks and where they are most likely to arise, you can decide which intellectual property legal services are worth buying. We discuss this problem further in When AI Tells You What Legal Work You Need.

What Your Business Owns and What Needs Protection

Most business IP falls into four categories: trademarks, patents, copyrights, and trade secrets. They protect different things, and confusing them leads to unnecessary spending.

What your business needs to protect Legal services worth considering
Brand names, logos, and product names Trademark clearance searches, registrations, enforcement
Inventions and new technology Patentability assessments, patent applications
Software, photographs, artwork, written content Copyright registration, ownership agreements, licensing
Formulas, processes, confidential business information Trade secret protection, confidentiality and non-use agreements
Product designs, molds, and tooling Manufacturing agreements, tooling ownership agreements, IP assignments
Technology shared with manufacturers or business partners NNN agreements, product development agreements, technology licensing
Work created by employees or contractors Employment and contractor IP assignment agreements

Before paying to protect IP, make sure you own it. Paying a contractor to develop software or design a product does not automatically transfer every intellectual property right to your company. Ownership depends on the work, applicable law, and the parties' agreements.

We see this problem with overseas manufacturers. A company pays for product development and assumes it owns the designs. Months later, it wants to change factories and discovers that its manufacturer claims ownership of the drawings, technology, or tooling. Our article on how companies give away their IP in China without realizing it describes how this happens. By the time lawyers get involved, the factory holds most of the leverage.

Where Your IP Needs Protection

Intellectual property rights are largely territorial. A U.S. trademark registration does not provide worldwide protection, and a U.S. patent does not ordinarily protect an invention against activities conducted entirely outside the United States. Yet companies regularly assume their U.S. trademark protects products manufactured in China because they sell only to American customers. It does not give them corresponding Chinese trademark rights. Our article on how to protect your IP internationally explains the broader considerations for businesses operating across borders.

China (and most of the rest of the world as well) is principally a first-to-file trademark country. Subject to exceptions, priority goes to the party that files first for the relevant mark and goods or services. Ten years of selling a branded product in the United States will not, by itself, prevent someone else from registering that brand in China.

We once dealt with an American company whose Chinese manufacturer registered 17 of its trademarks without permission, then offered the American company's customers the same products for 40 percent less. We describe that matter in How to Protect Your Trademarks as China Manufacturing Declines. In another matter, China Customs detained a major shipment belonging to a Canadian coat manufacturer because another company had registered its trademark in China. After reviewing the options and the cost of further delays, we negotiated the purchase of the trademark for six figures.

Companies manufacturing in China should register their core trademarks there, even if they never intend to sell to Chinese consumers. Someone else's Chinese registration can prevent them from manufacturing and exporting their own goods. That does not mean every company needs a Chinese-character trademark. If it sells only outside China, uses an English-language brand, and has no established Chinese name, a Chinese-character registration is usually an unnecessary expense. Protect the brand appearing on the goods and packaging first. We explain this in our guide to China trademark registrations.

The same reasoning applies elsewhere. Registration in a market you do not serve and have no plans to enter sometimes makes sense, but the expense needs a justification. I would rather see a company properly protect its most important trademark in three countries than scatter registrations across fifteen without knowing what each accomplishes. For companies considering registrations in multiple countries, our article on international trademark registration explains how the Madrid System works and what a single international application does and does not accomplish.

Which IP Protections Should Come First?

Most small and midsize businesses cannot afford every available IP protection. Their priorities depend on how they operate. A manufacturer, software developer, and consumer brand face different risks.

If You Manufacture Products Overseas

Suppose your U.S. company has designed a branded consumer product and found a Chinese factory willing to make it. Before buying legal services, determine what information the factory will receive, what it can do with that information, and how difficult switching manufacturers would be. If your brand is settled, file the China trademark application now. Our article on China NNN agreements versus trademark registrations explains why companies frequently need both forms of protection.

If you are approaching several factories with proprietary designs or valuable technical information, get a China NNN agreement signed before disclosure. Unlike a conventional American NDA, an NNN addresses unauthorized use and circumvention as well as disclosure. It protects you while evaluating prospective manufacturers, including those you reject.

After choosing a factory, you need a manufacturing agreement covering product specifications, quality standards, inspections, IP and tooling ownership, unauthorized subcontracting, and enforceable remedies. It should also prevent the factory from misusing your information and designs.

If you select your manufacturer before disclosing valuable information, and your manufacturing agreement contains the necessary non-disclosure, non-use, and non-circumvention provisions, you do not need a separate NNN. If you have already shared proprietary information under an NNN, the manufacturing agreement should address whether the earlier agreement remains effective and preserve rights arising from earlier disclosures and breaches. Your agreement with the chosen factory also does not bind rejected factories. See Do I Need a China NNN Agreement or a China Manufacturing Agreement? Usually Both.

Tooling needs protection too. One client paid $80,000 for molds, then paid its manufacturer $200,000 to recover them just eight months later. The production shutdown cost approximately $800,000 in lost revenue. The company had paid for the molds without securing its right to recover them. A proper mold and tooling agreement, or adequate tooling provisions in a manufacturing agreement, costs far less.

Make sure the contract binds the correct company. We routinely see Chinese manufacturers identified by English trade names rather than their registered Chinese legal names. Sometimes a Hong Kong trading company negotiates the deal while a mainland factory makes the products and holds the tooling. An excellent contract against the wrong company offers little practical protection. We explain why this matters in Why Accurate Chinese Company Names on Your Contracts Must Be Non-Negotiable.

For a broader discussion of trademarks, manufacturing contracts, and other protections, see How to Protect Your IP in China: Answers to the Questions Foreign Companies Ask Most.

If You Are Developing Software or Technology

Before worrying about international patents, a software company should examine its developer agreements. Do they transfer the necessary IP rights to the company and impose enforceable confidentiality obligations? Does the company understand restrictions on third-party code and control access to its source code? These questions become critical during investment or acquisition due diligence. Discovering that a former contractor owns important rights in your software can be expensive. Address ownership while the developers are still working with you.

Copyright protection arises automatically, but registration matters when infringement occurs. For a U.S. work, registration or refusal by the Copyright Office is ordinarily required before filing a federal infringement lawsuit. Subject to statutory exceptions, registering after infringement begins can prevent recovery of statutory damages and attorney fees. For published works, registering within three months after first publication can preserve eligibility for those remedies even when infringement begins before registration.

Early registration therefore makes sense for valuable software, photographs, artwork, and other works likely to be copied. It does not mean registering every piece of marketing material. Consider the work's value and exposure to infringement.

Patents require a separate assessment. A patent application makes sense when a qualifying invention provides an important competitive advantage, but international patent protection is expensive, and publication can disclose information that might otherwise remain secret. This work belongs with a patent specialist.

If You Are Launching a Consumer Brand

For many consumer businesses, trademarks take priority over patents. Begin with a clearance search to identify infringement risks and assess registrability, then determine the appropriate countries and trademark classes.

A protective-glove company came to us after China Customs detained its shipment. Its previous lawyer had registered its trademark in Class 25, which covers gloves worn as clothing. The client's protective work gloves belonged in Class 9. A competitor registered the mark for the relevant goods and used that registration to interfere with shipments. We discuss the matter in China Trademark Registration: Why U.S. Companies Need More Than a Filing Agent. The Chinese trademark lawyer had registered the trademark for gloves, as requested. What the client needed was someone who asked what kind of gloves it sold. A cheap filing covering the wrong products can be worse than no filing because it creates false confidence.

IP Legal Services You Can Skip

I wish more lawyers discussed unnecessary legal spending with prospective clients. A substantial number of companies asking us for China NNN agreements do not need them. Another form of protection works better, or the risk does not justify the cost. We have said this publicly for years, although drafting NNN agreements is part of our practice.

Small clothing companies are a good example. We almost never draft China NNN agreements for businesses sourcing ordinary apparel without disclosing valuable proprietary information. An NNN binds the factory that signs it. It does not bind the industry or prevent unrelated manufacturers from copying designs they are otherwise legally free to copy. Those manufacturers remain subject to applicable trademark, copyright, patent, and other IP laws, but they are not bound by your contract. Such companies usually need a China trademark for their brand before an NNN. The calculation changes when a company develops genuinely original designs or shares confidential technical information with prospective manufacturers.

Trademark applications offer another example. One company came to us after purchasing 11 China trademark applications from an online filing service when one would have covered its actual exposure. The extra applications provided no useful protection. We discuss this in our guide to China trademark registrations. Multiple registrations sometimes make sense, but each should address a real risk or business plan.

We also receive requests to review American NDAs and manufacturing contracts for use in China. We frequently decline because their governing-law provisions, dispute-resolution terms, and substantive protections were designed for another legal system. Reviewing them will not make them suitable China contracts. Starting with a contract drafted for the transaction and jurisdiction is usually more efficient. See China Manufacturing Contracts: Why Your Draft Does Not Work.

Companies also overspend on trade secret programs and foreign patents. A company with little valuable confidential information should question the need for an elaborate trade secret program. A startup should have a business reason before pursuing patents in numerous countries. Be skeptical of lawyers who recommend every available remedy without discussing its cost and likely value.

Choosing an IP Lawyer Who Understands Your Business

IP lawyers have different specialties. A patent lawyer who excels at pharmaceutical patents may have little experience negotiating Chinese manufacturing agreements. An international business lawyer experienced in trademarks and contracts should not prosecute complicated software patents. Trademark registration and trademark litigation also require different skills.

Firm size tells you little about whether a lawyer can handle your matter. A small IP boutique may be best for specialized patent work, and a solo practitioner can be excellent for routine filings. Foreign manufacturing, distribution, and licensing matters often call for international business experience. Our article, The High Cost of China Contract Mistakes, describes what can happen when companies hire lawyers without the necessary experience.

At Harris Sliwoski, much of our international IP practice involves protecting companies before they work with foreign businesses and helping them when those relationships go wrong. We have seen companies register trademarks while overlooking tooling ownership and sign confidentiality agreements that do nothing to prevent manufacturers from competing with them. Those experiences inform our advice about where clients should spend their legal budgets.

Questions to Ask Before Hiring an IP Lawyer

Spend less time asking how long a lawyer has practiced and more time asking how that lawyer would approach your business. My favorite question is "What would you protect first if this were your company?" Then ask why. A lawyer who recommends five trademark applications, two contracts, and an international patent strategy before learning about your business deserves skepticism.

I would also ask:

  • Have you handled this problem before? Request examples involving similar products, industries, or jurisdictions.
  • What would you tell us not to buy? The answer helps distinguish judgment from salesmanship.
  • How is our IP protection most likely to fail? This reveals whether the lawyer understands real disputes.
  • Who will handle our work? Determine who makes the important decisions and who performs the work.
  • What will we have when the work is finished? An application, registration, signed contract, and enforceable legal right are different things.
  • What will it cost if something goes wrong? Ask about refusals, oppositions, breaches, and enforcement.

A good lawyer should answer in language you understand. If you leave the consultation unsure what the lawyer proposes or why you need it, keep asking before hiring.

How IP Legal Fees Work

IP legal services are sold under several pricing arrangements. Routine filings and some contracts work well with flat fees. Litigation and complicated advisory work usually require hourly or phased billing. Monthly fixed fees sometimes make sense for ongoing portfolio management.

Fee structure Typical work Questions to ask
Flat fee Trademark filings, copyright registrations, standard agreements What is included, and what costs extra?
Hourly Litigation, complex licensing, specialized advice What is the estimated total cost, and when will it be updated?
Phased project fee IP audits, multi-country filings, complex transactions What does each phase deliver?
Monthly fixed fee Ongoing portfolio management and advice What services are included and excluded?

A Lower Quote Is Not Always a Better Deal

Suppose one firm quotes $1,000 for a trademark application and another quotes $2,000. The cheaper quote excludes clearance searches, government fees, and nearly all post-filing work, while the higher quote includes some or all of those services. Or perhaps only one firm understands which trademark classes cover your products. Remember the protective-glove company: it paid for a trademark registration without getting the protection it needed. There is also the question of judgment. A less expensive lawyer may lack the experience to distinguish what you need from what you don't, or may be more interested in generating fees than saving you money. You could end up paying for 11 trademark applications when one would have protected your business just as well.

Patent estimates require particular care. The initial filing cost does not tell you what you will spend responding to examiner objections, filing abroad, or maintaining issued patents. Find out which stages each estimate covers.

Get the Scope and Price in Writing Before Work Begins

Your engagement agreement should say exactly what you are buying. For trademarks, identify the marks, jurisdictions, classes, clearance searches, and government fees. Specify whether office action responses are included and what happens if someone opposes the application.

For manufacturing contracts, establish which agreements the firm will prepare, whether manufacturer verification is included, what languages will be used, which version controls, and whether the fee covers negotiations and revisions. Ask how the agreement will be made enforceable where the manufacturer operates.

The same principles apply to patents, IP ownership reviews, licensing, and litigation. Define the deliverables, your responsibilities, and the additional work requiring your approval. Distinguish the lawyer's preparation time from government processing time. A firm can file a trademark application promptly without controlling when or whether it is approved.

Agree in advance how unexpected work will be billed, including trademark conflicts, patent examiner rejections, and substantial contract revisions. Competent lawyers should be comfortable discussing these issues before starting. Before signing, make sure you understand what the firm will do, why your business needs it, what you will receive, and what you will pay. Resolve anything unclear before authorizing the work.

Frequently Asked Questions About IP Legal Services

How much does it cost to hire an intellectual property lawyer?

It depends on the work. Routine trademark filings and standard IP agreements are frequently handled for flat fees, while patent applications, complex licensing agreements, and IP disputes usually cost considerably more.

For international trademark registrations, we often tell clients to budget $2,000 per country, including all legal fees, government fees, and other costs, when deciding whether registration makes business sense. That figure is a reasonable estimate for many countries, though some cost less than $1,000 and others as much as $4,500.

Be careful when comparing quotes. A cheaper filing that excludes clearance searches, government fees, and follow-up work can ultimately cost more than a higher quote that includes them. Find out exactly what you are buying.

If I pay someone to develop my product, do I own the designs and tooling?

Not automatically. Paying a contractor or manufacturer for development work does not by itself transfer every intellectual property right to your company. Ownership depends on the work, applicable law, and the parties' agreements. Companies often discover this when they try to change factories and their manufacturer claims the drawings, technology, or molds.

One of our clients paid $80,000 for molds and eight months later paid its manufacturer $200,000 to recover them. The production shutdown cost approximately $800,000 in lost revenue. A proper tooling agreement, or adequate tooling provisions in your manufacturing agreement, costs far less. Make sure the agreement binds the company that actually holds the tooling under its registered Chinese legal name.

Does my U.S. trademark protect my brand in China?

No. Intellectual property rights are largely territorial, and a U.S. registration gives you no corresponding trademark rights in China, even if everything your factory makes ships to American customers. China is principally a first-to-file trademark country, so, subject to exceptions, priority goes to the party that files first for the relevant mark and goods or services.

Ten years of selling your brand in the United States will not, by itself, stop someone else from registering it in China. One American company's Chinese manufacturer registered 17 of its trademarks without permission and then offered its customers the same products for 40 percent less. Our China trademark registration guide explains how to protect your brand there.

Do I need a China trademark if I don't sell in China?

If you manufacture branded products in China, you should ordinarily register your core trademarks there. Someone else's Chinese registration can prevent you from manufacturing and exporting your own goods.

China Customs detained a major shipment belonging to a Canadian coat manufacturer because another company had registered its trademark in China. After weighing the options against the cost of further delays, we negotiated the purchase of that registration for six figures. Register the brand appearing on your goods and packaging first. A Chinese-character version is usually an unnecessary expense if you sell only outside China, use an English-language brand, and have no established Chinese name.

Do I need a China NNN agreement, a China manufacturing agreement, or both?

Usually both, and timing decides it. If you are approaching several factories with proprietary designs or valuable technical information, get an NNN signed before disclosure. It addresses unauthorized use and circumvention as well as disclosure, and protects you against factories you reject, which your eventual manufacturing agreement will not bind.

The manufacturing agreement with your chosen factory covers product specifications, quality standards, inspections, IP and tooling ownership, unauthorized subcontracting, and remedies. If you choose your manufacturer before sharing anything valuable, and your manufacturing agreement contains the necessary non-disclosure, non-use, and non-circumvention provisions, you do not need a separate NNN. We explain this in Do I Need a China NNN Agreement or a China Manufacturing Agreement? Usually Both.

Do I need to register my copyrights?

Will a China NNN agreement stop factories from copying my clothing designs?

It binds only the factories that are parties to the agreement. Other manufacturers remain subject to trademark, copyright, patent, and other IP laws, but your contract does not bind them, and they are free to copy designs the law otherwise lets them copy.

That is why we almost never draft China NNN agreements for small clothing companies sourcing ordinary apparel without disclosing valuable proprietary information. Those companies usually need a China trademark for their brand before an NNN. The calculation changes when a company develops genuinely original designs or shares confidential technical information with prospective manufacturers. See China NNN Agreements: What They Do, What They Don't, and How to Get Them Right.

Will you review my American NDA or manufacturing contract for use in China?

Starting with a contract drafted for the transaction and jurisdiction is usually more efficient. Whatever agreement you use should identify the manufacturer by its registered Chinese legal name, because an excellent contract against the wrong company offers little practical protection. We explain why in China Manufacturing Contracts: Why Your Draft Does Not Work.

Why do quotes for the same trademark filing vary so much?

Two quotes that look comparable often cover different work. A $1,000 trademark quote that excludes clearance searches, government fees, and nearly all post-filing work buys less than a $2,000 quote that includes those services. Quotes also reflect differences in the lawyers' experience and judgment.

A competitor registered the mark for the relevant goods and used it to interfere with the company's shipments. Before hiring anyone, get a written scope identifying the marks, countries, classes, included searches, government fees, and charges for responding to refusals or oppositions. For more on the glove case, see China Trademark Registration: Why U.S. Companies Need More Than a Filing Agent.

Can one lawyer handle trademarks, patents, copyrights, and international IP protection?

Some lawyers handle several areas of IP law, but few are equally experienced in all of them. Patent prosecution requires specialized qualifications, and negotiating an international manufacturing agreement calls for different experience from registering a trademark.

You do not need a separate law firm for every matter. An international business law firm can coordinate trademark protection, contracts, and foreign counsel while bringing in patent specialists when needed. Our firm, for example, does not draft utility patent applications. We bring in or refer clients to lawyers who specialize in that work. Ask who will actually handle each part of your matter.

Can I protect my intellectual property without hiring a lawyer?

Yes. You can file many trademark and copyright applications yourself and take steps to protect confidential information. The risk is paying for the wrong protection or overlooking something important.

articles.title: China Domain Name and Trademark Scam Emails
articles.content:
An email arrives from China warning that someone is about to register your company's name. Sometimes it comes from a supposed domain registrar claiming another business wants your name as a Chinese domain. Other times, a Chinese intellectual property firm says someone has applied to register your trademark and that you have only a short time to oppose it. Our China lawyers have dealt with hundreds of these emails over the past two decades. Most have been scams or sales solicitations, but some trademark warnings identify genuine applications with real deadlines. Either way, do not reply to the sender and do not pay it. Check the claim yourself or through your own lawyer.
Companies that paid these senders spent anywhere from $500 to $3,500. Roughly a third were simply ghosted. Another third were ghosted and then, within a few weeks, someone tried to hold their trademark for ransom, usually for $10,000 or more. Only the last third had paid a real law firm or trademark agent that challenged the registration as promised and then filed a trademark application for the company. Those are bad odds for a problem you can check yourself.
The domain-name version has been circulating for more than 20 years. When we first wrote about it in 2009, our lawyers had already seen at least fifty of these emails, and we have reviewed many more since then. The wording changes, but the sender usually claims another company has applied to register your company name, product name, or trademark under China's .cn or .中国 domain extensions, sometimes along with .hk or other Asian domains.
The supposed registrar says it has discovered a conflict with your existing name and wants to know whether the applicant is your distributor, business partner, or authorized representative. The email suggests you have only a short time to stop the registration. If you object, the sender offers to register the domains for you, often at inflated prices or with expensive multiyear commitments. Other versions claim the domains have already been registered and offer to arrange their transfer for a fee.
These emails are generally sales pitches disguised as trademark protection notices. Ordinary domain registration is not a trademark-clearance proceeding in which a registrar must obtain permission from every business that might have rights in a similar name. The China Internet Network Information Center (CNNIC) generally operates .cn registration on a first-come, first-served basis, subject to applicable registration requirements and restrictions. An unfamiliar company's claim that it must consult you before processing someone else's application gives you no reason to believe the application exists.
Years ago, when more American businesspeople were traveling to China, we noticed something odd. Some of these emails arrived a week or two after someone returned from a China trip. It happened often enough that we wondered how the senders knew which companies to contact, though we never established where they obtained their information. Whoever they were targeting got scared. Much of the time we would run a search, find no filings, tell the client it should get a China trademark anyway, and then get it for them.
One of our lawyers received the following email, which her email system had already placed in its spam folder. The sender claimed to be protecting the recipient against an unauthorized registration. It provided no evidence that anyone had actually applied for the domain.
We are China’s internet domain services company, and last week, we received an application from a Chinese company that has requested “Example USA Company” as their internet name and China (.CN) domain name. But after checking into it, we learned that this name conflicts with your company name or trademark. To deal with this matter better, it’s necessary to send an email to you and confirm whether this company is your distributor or business partner in China and to confirm that you authorized this domain registration Please respond soonest.
Another version makes the supposed threat seem larger by listing several Asian domain extensions. It also identifies a purported applicant, which can make the message appear more credible. Here is another actual example we received:
I am grateful for you checking this letter out. We are a Chinese domain registrar. Recently, we received a registration request from “ABC Technology Ltd” applying to register Example brand and domain names(.cn, .hk, etc.), which have the same main body as your company’s name. We are sending this letter to confirm with your company whether you authorize them to register those names. Please give me your thoughts ASAP to let us carry on, Thanks.
The .cn extension belongs to mainland China's domain system, while .hk is Hong Kong's country-code domain and operates under separate rules. Listing them together establishes neither a genuine application nor a legal conflict. Both emails rely on the recipient's fear that another company is about to take something valuable. Neither supplies information that would justify paying the sender or disclosing details about your company's customers, suppliers, or distributors.
The trademark version is more complicated because it often refers to a genuine legal procedure. These emails usually come from someone claiming to work for a Chinese law firm, trademark agency, or intellectual property research company. The sender says another business has applied to register a mark identical or similar to yours, that the application has been published in China's Trademark Gazette, and that the deadline for filing an opposition is approaching.
A typical email looks like this:
Dear [owner of US trademark]:
According to our trademark research team, the following mark has been published in the Chinese Trademark Gazette on [date]. We note that this mark is identical to a registration owned by your company.
[details of allegedly published mark]
The Chinese Trademark Office has already completed its examination of this mark and the mark is now open to opposition until [deadline]. The deadline is not extendable. If no one files an opposition before the deadline, the mark will proceed to registration.
Please let us know if we can be of assistance in opposing this mark.
[name of Chinese IP firm]
This email deserves more careful treatment than the domain-registration warning because it describes a real procedure. China publishes trademark applications that have passed preliminary examination, and eligible parties can oppose them during a limited period. Under the law in effect through December 31, 2026, that period is three months from publication. China's revised Trademark Law, adopted in June 2026 and effective January 1, 2027, reduces the opposition period to two months. The applicable deadline for a particular application must be determined under the governing law and the application's publication records.
The shorter deadline makes it more important for companies with valuable Chinese trademarks to monitor new applications rather than depend on unsolicited warnings. We explain the practical consequences in Five Practical Steps Foreign Brands Should Take to Prepare for China's New Trademark Law. A company that first learns of a conflicting application near the end of its opposition period has little time to investigate the applicant, evaluate its legal position, and prepare an opposition.
Some unsolicited trademark emails identify applications that actually exist. Some come from legitimate Chinese law firms or trademark agents that will perform the work they offer. That does not establish that the recipient has valid grounds to oppose the application or that an opposition is worth the expense. It also does not mean the sender is the right person to retain.
These senders email thousands of companies and make their money from the few that answer. Filing for the brand of a company that ignores them makes no economic sense, but a company that writes back worried has just shown it will pay to keep its name. Answering one of these emails, especially the trademark version, greatly increases your odds of ending up with a real China trademark problem. Even with the real law firms and trademark agents, it sometimes seemed they tried to register the name only after they knew they had a client who would pay to challenge it.
The sensible response is to have a China trademark lawyer you choose check the application promptly. If the application exists and threatens your rights, the opposition deadline matters, and waiting can limit your options. You have no reason to engage the person who sent the email in order to conduct that investigation.
Do not respond to the sender at all. Avoid payment links and unexpected attachments, and do not provide business documents, passwords, or registrar-account information. Responding confirms that your email address is active and that the subject interests you, which can invite more solicitations. You can investigate a legitimate domain or trademark problem without involving the person who contacted you.
A stranger's demand for an immediate answer means nothing. A genuine trademark opposition deadline, however, is a different matter and needs prompt verification. If a message claims that a domain you already own is about to expire, check its status by logging directly into your account with your actual registrar. Renewal problems can be serious, but an unexpected email is not a reliable source for determining whether one exists.
Start with the exact domains named in the email.
example.cn,
example.com.cn, and
example.中国 are different registrations, and a warning mentioning all three does not mean any of them has been taken. Check any Chinese-language version of your brand that customers actually use. A domain the sender wants you to purchase may be entirely unregistered.
For .cn and .中国 domains, use CNNIC's official WHOIS lookup to check whether the domain has been registered. CNNIC also provides registration instructions and information on authorized registrars. For generic domains such as .com and .net, use ICANN's Registration Data Lookup. An established registrar you select independently can also help determine whether the names are available.
These searches can show whether a domain is registered, which registrar manages it, and what ownership information is publicly available. Some registrant information is withheld, and registration databases do not necessarily disclose applications that have not been completed. If a search identifies an existing registration, preserve the date and other available information. Check how the domain is being used, bearing in mind that a domain can be configured for email even when it has no visible website.
If a domain is available and genuinely important to your business, register it through a reputable provider. You do not need to purchase it through the person who sent the warning. For .cn domains, use a registrar familiar with CNNIC's registration and identity-verification requirements.
China's official trademark records can be searched through the China National Intellectual Property Administration's trademark search system. A search can identify applications, registrations, applicants, publication dates, and the goods or services involved. CNIPA's public database is not updated in real time, so the absence of an application from a search does not conclusively establish that nothing has been filed.
Your own China trademark lawyer should determine whether a particular application exists, which marks and goods it covers, and whether your company has legally sufficient grounds and standing to oppose it. If an opposition is warranted, counsel needs to act within the applicable deadline. A published application that threatens an important brand deserves attention even when the person who notified you has no legitimate reason to be involved.
If the application described in the email cannot be verified, there is no reason to pay the sender for an opposition. Your lawyer's search may nevertheless reveal that your business should be registering its own marks. The domain-name version has been circulating for more than 20 years. The .cn extension belongs to mainland China's domain system, while .hk is Hong Kong's country-code domain and operates under separate rules. articles.title: Moving Manufacturing From China to Mexico
articles.content:
When China's COVID-zero lockdowns and its aggression toward Taiwan started spooking foreign companies in 2022, the international manufacturing lawyers at my firm began getting a steady stream of calls and emails from companies looking to leave China. Most wanted to know about Mexico, and some of the companies calling us were themselves Chinese or Taiwanese. The tariff wars since then have given companies more reasons to look south. Mexico makes sense for many of them. But companies that go into Mexico expecting to find China with a shorter shipping route are in for an expensive education.
Starting in 2022, my good friend Andrew Hupert and I wrote a long series of posts for this blog on what leaving China for Mexico actually involves. Nobody was better suited to write about this than Andrew. I first met him in Shanghai in 2003, and over the following two decades I came to rely deeply on his practical business wisdom, especially about China. When my firm stepped up its China practice, he was one of my go-to people on all things China. He was a business school professor who taught negotiation around the world, and he spent more than 20 years in Asia, living and working in Shanghai, Taipei, Hong Kong, and Saigon. Though he had tied his career to China, he, like me, was an early believer in a post-China manufacturing world. He moved to Thailand and then Vietnam, and when Mexico began emerging as a leading replacement for China manufacturing, he moved to Monterrey and then Oaxaca, and became fluent in Spanish. He spent his last years there helping companies, especially companies leaving China, set up and run operations in Mexico. Few people had spent as much time thinking about how the two countries compared, and fewer still had Andrew's willingness to say exactly what he thought.
Andrew died of a heart attack in Oaxaca in October 2024, at 61. I wrote about him and our friendship in Remembering Andrew Hupert. This guide brings our Mexico work together in one place and updates it for 2026. Most of the business and cultural observations are Andrew's, drawn from his years running and advising operations in both countries. The legal and trade analysis is mine, informed by my firm's affiliated lawyers in Mexico City and the United States, and by many of the conclusions Andrew and I reached together over the years. Andrew is no longer here to update his words, so I have done that as best I can. Where events have proved us right or wrong, I say so. When I quote him, the words are his as he wrote them. I want readers to understand where his observations came from and why I continue to think they matter.
In early 2023, Andrew and I wrote that running a supply chain entirely through China had become a bet against the house, the kind that ends with the gambler up a ton at midnight and borrowing bus fare home by morning. The trade numbers seemed to argue otherwise. U.S.-China trade had hit a record $690 billion in 2022, and plenty of companies took that as vindication of their decision to stay. Multinationals were reading the situation differently. Their supply chain planners, the Lean Production and Six Sigma people who treat unnecessary risk as a sin, were piling into Mexico, as Unilever's $400 million commitment to a new plant in Nuevo León showed that same month. When a Chinese surveillance balloon was shot down over the United States that February, we predicted that cooler heads would not prevail. Washington, we said, would keep changing the economics of China supply chains by every means available, and Beijing would answer each new U.S. restriction with its own. We saw little reason to expect either government to put the interests of companies caught in the middle ahead of its own political priorities.
We put governments at the top of the list of likely supply chain shocks and said the damage would most likely come through mistakes, meaning bad regulations written and enforced for non-economic goals. Would governments knowingly hurt their own economies for a good soundbite? "Yes. Of course they would. We expected U.S. customs to demand ever more detailed proof that your goods were not made with forced labor in Xinjiang. Complying would trap your China staff in a catch-22, because trying to trace the origin of your materials could get them "invited to tea" by the authorities. We also expected Beijing to retaliate, since, as we put it, "Beijing will not apologize; it will reply." China has a long record of using trade to punish countries that anger it, including Japan, Norway, Canada, South Korea, Australia, and Lithuania. And we warned that after the disruptions of 2021 and 2022, no owner or fiduciary could credibly claim a China supply chain disruption was impossible to foresee. Many of our clients already had China exit and evacuation plans, and we told readers they should too. That advice was based on what we were already seeing companies struggle with, long before the current tariff battles. See Doing Business with China and Your Reputation Risks and Repeat After Me: Trade Relations Between the United States and China Will Only Get Worse.
Tariffs and trade restrictions have since vindicated much of what we wrote. In 2023, Mexico overtook China as the top source of U.S. goods imports, at $475.6 billion to China's $427.2 billion, with China's total down 20 percent from 2022. Real U.S. imports from China fell 28 percent in 2025 alone, and by year-end the average U.S. tariff on Chinese goods was near 50 percent, up from 21 percent when the second Trump administration took office. Beijing retaliated most effectively with rare earth export controls. It suspended its expanded October 2025 controls for one year, until November 10, 2026, but its April 2025 controls on seven medium and heavy rare earths remain in force. The forced-labor scrutiny we predicted has also become a basis for tariffs. In July 2026, the U.S. Trade Representative imposed tariffs on goods from 60 economies, China and Mexico among them, after finding that they had failed to impose and effectively enforce bans on imports made with forced labor. Our biggest mistake was assuming North American trade would remain politically protected. We underestimated just how willing Washington would be to make life difficult for companies manufacturing in Mexico, a subject I discuss below.
Companies that left China early told us their decisions had paid off. In that same 2023 series, Andrew and I passed along what clients who had moved their manufacturing elsewhere were saying. One said he slept better, both because he worried less about his supply chain and because he felt better about no longer supporting such a brutal regime. Another had left before COVID, which let it avoid the China tariffs, underprice its competitors, and take a good chunk of market share while those competitors scrambled to catch up. Others said they were hiring people who chose them because they had nothing to do with China. Still others had customers choosing them because their products did not come from China, whether to reduce supply chain risk or reputational risk. These were business owners explaining what had happened to their companies, and their experiences were far more persuasive than another consultant's presentation about geopolitical risk. We also said the most unforgivable sin foreign companies committed in China was going there without an exit strategy. I still believe that, and I would build an exit strategy into any Mexico plan from the start as well.
One of the most important differences between manufacturing in China and Mexico is how much control you have over the risks your business faces. Every country has problems. Factories lose power, employees leave, suppliers fail, and shipments get delayed. You can reduce many of these risks by investigating your suppliers, choosing your location carefully, and making sure you have alternative sources of supply. You can never eliminate every manufacturing risk, but there is a great deal you can do to keep ordinary business problems from becoming disasters.
Many of Mexico's biggest manufacturing risks fall into that category. Security is a serious concern, but you can investigate specific locations and arrange safer transportation. Labor laws are demanding, but you can hire Mexican employment lawyers and structure your operation to comply with them. Infrastructure varies considerably, but you can check whether a proposed site has reliable power and water before committing to it. None of these precautions guarantees that your operation will run smoothly. They do, however, give you meaningful ways to reduce your exposure.
China presents some risks that no amount of good management can bring under your control. You can investigate your suppliers and trace your materials, but you cannot eliminate the possibility that U.S. Customs will detain your goods over forced-labor concerns. You cannot prevent Beijing from imposing export restrictions or Washington from raising tariffs. You can prepare for a crisis involving Taiwan, but you cannot prevent one. A company can do everything right inside its Chinese factory and still find its business badly damaged by a political decision made thousands of miles away. That is what makes these risks especially troubling. The company has very little ability to influence the decisions that create them.
Mexico has political risks of its own, as the 2026 USMCA review and the latest tariffs demonstrate. A Mexican manufacturer cannot control what Washington decides about North American trade any more than a Chinese manufacturer can control U.S. policy toward China. I would never suggest otherwise. But when comparing countries, I would pay particular attention to which risks you can realistically manage and which ones can overwhelm your business regardless of how carefully you operate. That distinction is one of the strongest reasons many companies have decided they would rather manufacture in Mexico.
Andrew's test turned on what you make and who buys it. Several kinds of companies can probably stay in China: those that provide services to Chinese B2B markets, produce for sale in China and Asia, or specialize in multinational supply chains. Companies that depend on an end-to-end global presence, such as hotels, travel companies, and financial services firms, can also stay, as can those big enough to run separate supply chains for separate markets. Companies that need materials, components, technology, or processes available only in China are a maybe. Their position keeps deteriorating, and nobody should want to be the last international manufacturer in China. A company running a low-cost strategy built on small runs of pre-sold products, less-than-container-load shipping, probably cannot stay. The important question is whether your own business falls into one of the categories that still makes economic sense there.
Andrew's starting point, from the first post of our series, was that comparing China and Mexico is not comparing apples to apples. The same product may leave the factory gate in both countries, but setting up and running operations in them involves very different systems. China's economy is highly structured and centrally planned. Mexico's is decentralized and reactive, and much of what China's government arranged for you, you arrange yourself in Mexico. Had you matched the two head to head on operational effectiveness and site selection in 2010, China would have won handily. But Mexico is becoming a major commercial and manufacturing center, but it is not trying to be the factory of the world. It offers excellent trade access and an emerging-market cost structure, though getting started there is rarely quick or easy. Companies accustomed to China's manufacturing infrastructure need to understand just how much work Mexico expects them to do themselves. The learning curve is steep, even for companies that have spent decades manufacturing overseas.
Andrew liked to illustrate the difference with his Shanghai years. China earned its factory-of-the-world title at the start of the century, when anyone with a widget design scrawled on a napkin and a few thousand dollars could get it made. Much of that came from tightly integrated clusters of manufacturers and distributors bound together by informal personal relationships. When something went wrong, four or five engineers would huddle in a stairwell with a pack of Zhongnanhais. Twenty minutes later they came back with a workaround, a part they had sent the youngest team member pedaling off to get, and the name of the guy nearby with the machine or know-how they needed. Andrew saw that sort of informal problem-solving so often that he came to regard it as a defining feature of China's manufacturing system.
Mexico does things differently. Glitches and supply chain adjustments go up through established official channels, often running through Dallas, Detroit, or Deerfield, Illinois. Mexico is a world of ISO 9000-series certifications and the Toyota Way, and its factory managers treat verifiable performance as the only valid proof of a process. We used to describe business in China with an old expression, "Everything is possible, but nothing is easy." Mexican managers do not say this. A Chinese factory will take a job if it is reasonably sure it can do it, and in China someone is always willing to take your money and then figure out how to meet your requirements. A Mexican factory manager will turn down projects that feel improvised or hard to replicate. He or she will expect you to arrive with a complete operating plan covering your product, supply chain, bill of materials, and sources. Companies accustomed to the improvisation of Shenzhen or Dongguan often have trouble understanding why a Mexican factory refuses a project that looks perfectly manageable to them.
Andrew and I put it bluntly in 2023. The international brands succeeding in Mexico show up with capital, equipment, a supply chain, and above all a plan. Early China entrants could figure things out on the ground or lean on their factory to figure things out for them. That approach generally fails in Mexico, where the expectation is that you have already figured out how your product will be made. Companies that have spent years letting a Chinese factory fill the gaps in their plans often discover that most of their own specifications live in the factory's files, not theirs. In return for that rigor, the projects that do go forward tend to be well managed, because it is unusual to invest in Mexico without an independent feasibility study and business plan.
Start with your industry. Andrew's rule of thumb was that a company making the right kind of product (autos and auto parts, aerospace, or labor-intensive goods) the right way (through a wholly owned subsidiary) for sale in the United States can boost its profits in Mexico and "rescue what's left of your sanity." Companies that assemble electronics, produce medical devices or EV and green technologies, or make furniture or certain textiles can do well there too, though they will have to put together pieces China already provides. The closer your existing operation is to a fully documented production process that you control, the easier the transition usually becomes.
Production people in Mexico told Andrew they distinguish between companies that are "production-ready" and "companies with products." You are production-ready if you control your own production process, sourcing, and logistics and have the molds, the IP, the supplier list, and the data needed to start production yourself. Production-ready companies send operations specialists who arrive with detailed information on the product, the parts, the process, and the people, and they want Mexican partners to build facilities, handle regulations, and help with staffing, accounting, payroll, and HR. They are usually in autos, aerospace, or large-scale assembly, and there is a good chance they already have facilities in Mexico. Mexico's standards here were set by the maquiladoras along the border, essentially U.S. factories that happen to be in Mexico. GM, Caterpillar, Ford, and other heavy hitters of process engineering run plants there with engineering standards that are very high and, by China standards, not very flexible.
Our clients who go to Mexico with an established process have done well there. Our clients who do not really know manufacturing have not.
If you are willing to invest in your own production or assembly operation, you can probably find people to help you source materials and set up production. You will face a Catch-22, though. The people you hire to help you figure everything out will expect you to supply plans, answers, and solutions on the very topics you know least, and they prefer a tried-and-true solution everyone understands beforehand. You are also hiring your own factory management. The local version of the guy who took care of things for you in Shenzhen is now on your payroll and looking to you for ideas. Andrew saw an upside for China veterans, whose time in Asia gives them a talent for spotting opportunities and underdeveloped relationships. The downside is that ideas that seem mundane to you may get indifferent shrugs from Mexican managers who see no point in innovating for innovation's sake. You can make this model work, though you should budget for far more management time and preparation than you needed when your Chinese manufacturer was handling most of the details.
Plenty of plucky entrepreneurs built brands in China on "virtual factories" that were really just a string of contract manufacturing agreements. You can probably still do that in Shenzhen. You never could in Mexico, and you almost certainly won't be able to anytime soon. If your business depends on small quantities, customized output, and low-cost materials, you have been relying on production and logistics features unique to China. Your small runs ride on the tail end of a larger customer's order or fill excess capacity in busy production centers, and that kind of short-term, informal access to capacity is rare in Mexico. Start with a feasibility check before you spend money on anything else. There is little point in negotiating Mexican factory prices until you know whether the sort of manufacturing arrangement that made your China business possible even exists there.
Small and midsize businesses need to be particularly careful here. A large multinational can afford to build a factory, hire local management, and absorb production problems while it gets things working. A smaller company usually has far less money available for mistakes and often depends heavily on one manufacturer. Losing that supplier or discovering that a Mexican operation requires much more capital than expected can put the entire business at risk. If you have spent years relying on a Chinese factory to handle production for you, find out what replacing that arrangement will actually involve before committing to Mexico.
Contract manufacturing exists in Mexico, and on a large scale in some industries. Electronics manufacturing services companies run big plants around Guadalajara and along the border, and plenty of plastics, metal, and assembly shops serve automakers and appliance makers. What Mexico lacks is China's ecosystem of factories that will take a sketch, a small order, and a modest deposit and figure out the rest. Mexican contract manufacturers generally want established customers with complete technical packages, predictable volumes, and real commitments. The vocabulary is different too. Andrew found that people in Mexico often used "OEM" to mean a wholly owned subsidiary. He once visited a Caterpillar plant in Coahuila that the locals called an OEM, though he would call it a subsidiary, since it was a Caterpillar plant with Caterpillar employees making products only for Caterpillar. For most small and midsize companies leaving China, the realistic choices are a shelter arrangement or your own subsidiary, both discussed below. Companies that insist on finding the Mexican equivalent of their Chinese contract manufacturer can spend a great deal of time looking for something that simply is not there.
Whichever arrangement you choose, investigate the companies you will be relying on before you commit. That means confirming that a proposed manufacturer or shelter company actually has the facilities and resources it claims to have, and finding out whether it has a history of disputes or financial problems. Look at who owns the business and whether it has experience handling the kind of production you need. Do not assume that a polished presentation or an impressive industrial park address tells you much about the company itself. See our Foreign Company Due Diligence Reports practice page.
Andrew and I warned in 2023 that the alternatives were filling up. Vietnam works for many companies, but by then many of its factories and logistics providers were at capacity, and a call from Samsung gets local officials moving in a way a call from a midsize company does not. Vietnam's tariff edge over China has also narrowed. Since July 2026, Vietnamese goods pay the same 12.5 percent forced-labor tariff as Chinese goods, though not the older China-specific tariffs. India is rising but remains a very difficult place to do business, and many of the companies we worked with that went into India left within a year. We have many clients who love Guatemala for making cotton goods and some food items, but not much else. Colombia, El Salvador, and Peru are showing up more and more, but reviews for more complicated products tend to be mixed. Mexico suits brands selling into the United States and companies in those supply chains, but it too has been filling up, mostly with expansions by companies already there, like Toyota. None of these countries is an automatic substitute for China. You need to determine which one works for your particular products, customers, and way of manufacturing, and you need to do that before you make commitments you cannot easily undo.
The tariff picture has whipsawed. In February 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the president had exceeded his authority by imposing tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. The White House ended the emergency tariffs it had tied to drugs and migration at the southern border that same day. A temporary global 10 percent surcharge under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 replaced them. When it expired on July 24, 2026, the Section 301 forced-labor tariffs took effect. Chinese goods now pay an additional 12.5 percent, on top of the Section 301 tariffs first imposed on Chinese goods in 2018, which run from 7.5 to 100 percent depending on the product. Mexican goods pay an additional 10 percent, except goods entered duty-free under the USMCA and products already covered by Section 232. Section 232 tariffs of up to 50 percent on steel, aluminum, and copper apply even to USMCA-qualifying goods. A USMCA-qualifying car still pays the 25 percent auto tariff on its non-U.S. content. These overlapping measures make it dangerous to rely on a general statement about what tariffs apply to goods made in either country. The answer depends on the product and how it qualifies under the applicable rules.
A product made in Mexico that qualifies under the USMCA generally enters the United States duty-free, unless it is steel, aluminum, copper, or a car. The same product made in China generally pays the additional 12.5 percent, unless an exclusion applies, on top of its regular duty and any older Section 301 tariff. That gap is the strongest argument for Mexico, and it depends entirely on USMCA qualification. Product-specific exclusions and classifications matter, so run the numbers for your own products. I would never recommend moving production based on a headline tariff comparison without first establishing exactly how U.S. Customs will classify and treat the finished goods.
The USMCA itself is less settled than when Andrew and I started writing. At its first joint review on July 1, 2026, the United States declined to renew the agreement in its current form, while confirming it stays in force pending resolution of the issues or termination. That triggers annual joint reviews until the parties agree to an extension or the agreement expires on July 1, 2036, and USTR has opened public consultation for the 2027 review. Any party can withdraw on six months' notice. U.S.-Mexico negotiations remain unresolved. The fourth bilateral round, planned for Washington in September, slipped into October, and Mexican officials said in early October that a deal cutting U.S. tariffs on Mexican steel and aluminum was close. Nothing has been signed. Companies making long-term investments in Mexico therefore need to pay attention to the negotiations, even if their products currently qualify for favorable treatment.
A factory you expect to run for fifteen years now sits under a trade agreement reviewed every year. At least one prominent trade analyst expects most companies to respond by putting their plans on hold. Mexico still drew a record $40.87 billion in foreign direct investment in 2025, driven largely by reinvested earnings, which fits Andrew's view that Mexico favors companies that already know how to operate there. I would not build a Mexico business case that only works if the USMCA stays exactly as it is, and I would not let the review freeze you either. Nothing in the review so far points toward the United States making Chinese goods cheaper relative to Mexican goods. What I would do is test the investment against less favorable tariff assumptions and decide whether the economics still justify moving ahead.
Early on, many companies were coming to our international trade lawyers after setting up in Mexico expecting major tariff savings. Only then do they learn that their products would not qualify as made in Mexico or, even if they did, would still face substantial tariffs. Moving final assembly to Mexico while continuing to buy most of your components from China does not make your product Mexican. We would much rather have that conversation before the company commits to a factory, because by then the options for fixing the problem are usually much better. Fortunately, more companies understand this now.
Two separate questions are involved, and they follow different rules. Whether a product enters the United States duty-free under the USMCA turns on the agreement's product-specific rules of origin. Those rules generally require that non-North American inputs undergo a specified tariff classification change in North America and, for many products, that a minimum share of the product's value be regional. The auto rules show how demanding this can get. Under NAFTA, a car or truck qualified if 62.5 percent of its content came from the three member countries. The USMCA raised that to 75 percent and added a labor rule requiring that 40 to 45 percent of a vehicle's content come from workers earning at least $16 an hour. You need to apply the rules to the actual components and production process of your product, rather than assume that performing a certain amount of work in Mexico is enough.
Under 19 CFR Part 102 rules (which CBP formally applied to Section 301 determinations for Mexican and Canadian imports in 2021), origin is determined by specific tariff-shift requirements rather than a general substantial transformation test. While Part 102 standardizes country-of-origin marking and Section 301 treatment, simple assembly of Chinese parts in Mexico that fails the required Part 102 tariff shift will leave the product subject to Section 301 tariffs upon entry into the United States. A countertop appliance whose motor, circuit board, and housing all come from Guangdong does not become Mexican simply because workers in Monterrey fit the pieces together and box it.
Declare it Mexican anyway and you face back duties and potential penalties. Before you commit, get a binding ruling from U.S. Customs and Border Protection on your product's origin. I would want that answer in hand before making any significant investment that depends on escaping the China tariffs. See U.S. Customs Compliance: Your Ultimate Guide to Avoiding Costly Delays, Penalties, and Seizures and Why Following Your Chinese Supplier's Tariff Advice Could Land YOU in Jail.
The Trump administration has repeatedly accused Mexico of being a "back door" for Chinese products, and the USMCA review has increased scrutiny of whether goods processed in Mexico genuinely qualify for USMCA treatment. If your company is Chinese-owned, build your origin and compliance documentation as though U.S. Customs will audit it, and plan on the rules for Chinese content in North American goods getting tighter. The political attention directed at Chinese investment in Mexico makes careful documentation especially important, regardless of how legitimate your manufacturing operation is.
Effective January 1, 2026, Mexico raised import duties on more than 1,400 tariff lines, at rates from 5 to 50 percent, on goods from countries with no trade agreement with Mexico. The covered goods include autos, auto parts, textiles, clothing, plastics, and steel, and most face rates of up to 35 percent. China is the main target, but the tariffs also hit South Korea, India, Indonesia, Russia, Thailand, Türkiye, Taiwan, and Brazil. A second decree in April 2026 added 185 more tariff lines, and the first decree is written to run through December 31, 2026. Companies that planned their Mexico operations using the older Mexican tariff schedules need to recalculate their costs before relying on those earlier numbers.
Mexico's IMMEX program, which people use interchangeably with maquiladora, lets manufacturers bring in materials for export production without paying import duties. Companies certified for VAT purposes also get a credit offsetting the VAT on those imports. Many companies assume that protects them from Mexico's new duties. Where most of you will operate, it doesn't. USMCA Article 2.5 caps IMMEX duty deferral on non-North American materials used in products exported to the United States or Canada at the lesser of the Mexican duty on those materials or the U.S. or Canadian duty on the finished goods. If your finished product enters the United States duty-free, there is little or nothing to offset. A maquiladora can owe the full Mexican tariff on a Chinese part that goes into a U.S.-bound product. Mexico's PROSEC sectoral programs can reduce the Mexican duty on some non-North American inputs, but they are no blanket fix. Chinese inputs now get taxed at the Mexican border and put the finished product's USMCA status at risk at the U.S. border, so run the tariff math at both borders before you sign a lease. A company that looks only at the U.S. duty on its finished product can miss a substantial part of what its new Mexican production arrangement will cost.

Mexico's relatively weak central government means each state has developed its own industrial strengths, largely independent of national policy. Guadalajara, in Jalisco, is the Silicon Valley of Mexico. Saltillo and Monterrey anchor autos, appliances, and heavy industry in the northeast, and the Bajío states of Querétaro, Guanajuato, and Aguascalientes host auto and aerospace clusters. The border cities from Tijuana to Matamoros remain the heart of maquiladora assembly. Ports, highways, and rail lines decide where industry goes, so you have many options, but you have to research and organize your own facilities. Choosing a Mexican location requires far more attention to the specific requirements of your manufacturing operation than simply deciding which city has the lowest wages. See our Mexico Law practice page.
Infrastructure deserves more scrutiny than most companies give it. Mexico's industrial park association identifies energy supply as one of the main infrastructure constraints on nearshoring in 2026. Water is a real issue in parts of the north, as Monterrey's shortages in 2022 showed. The busiest industrial corridors compete hard for skilled workers. Before you sign a lease or buy land, confirm the available power, water, workforce, transportation links, and land-use and environmental permits for the specific site. Also ask whether it falls in one of the government's new incentive zones. Under Plan México, the government has designated Polos de Desarrollo Económico para el Bienestar, development zones that offer tax incentives through 2030, including an extra 25 percent deduction for research and development and training. Zones include a site in Ciudad Juárez focused on electromobility, semiconductors, and medical devices. The existence of a government incentive should never substitute for determining whether the location actually works for your manufacturing needs.
Mexico's security risks are real business risks, and companies need to evaluate them as seriously as any other operating cost. Organized crime extortion of businesses in Mexico has grown in scope and target size. Cargo theft fell 21 percent in the first five months of 2026, but attacks have turned more violent, with at least 14 truck drivers killed this year. Eighty-two percent of 2025 truck cargo thefts involved violence. The State of Mexico and Puebla account for the largest share of incidents, and Jalisco has become a major hotspot. I would reject both the idea that every part of Mexico is too dangerous for manufacturing and the equally foolish assumption that these problems will never affect your business.
Foreign manufacturers operate successfully in Mexico every day, and the better-run ones make security part of their operating plan. They look at the actual risks for their facilities and transportation routes instead of relying on national crime statistics or general impressions of a city. At a minimum, that means:
For many product companies, a shelter company is the most realistic way to start, and Chinese manufacturers use the same route to get into Mexico fast. A Mexican shelter company provides the legal entity, the IMMEX registration, the workforce on its payroll, and the customs, tax, and labor compliance. You supply the equipment, materials, and production know-how, and you run the manufacturing. You pay a fee and get into production without first building a Mexican company from scratch. That arrangement can make an enormous difference for a company entering Mexico for the first time, especially one that needs to get production running without spending months building its own administrative operation.
A shelter arrangement still leaves you with legal and operational risks that need to be addressed before you sign. Mexico's 2021 outsourcing reform sharply restricts personnel subcontracting and permits only specialized services or works under defined rules. The choice among a shelter, a direct subsidiary, and specialized service providers can therefore determine who carries labor-law exposure and whether the model works under current rules. You also give up a measure of direct control, because your workers and your compliance sit inside someone else's company. Those are serious considerations when you are deciding how your operation will function over the next several years.
Say a midsize outdoor gear company starts production in Querétaro through a shelter company. The arrangement works well for three years, and the company decides to form its own Mexican subsidiary. Only then does it read its shelter agreement closely. The agreement says nothing about who owns the improvements made to its production line or how its equipment and inventory leave the shelter's IMMEX program. Nor does it say how its 150 workers move to the new company with their seniority and benefits intact. Every one of those questions is now a negotiation with a counterparty that has no reason to make it easy. Your shelter agreement should settle them at the start, covering who owns the equipment and IP, who is liable for what, how you get your assets out, and how the workforce transfers. You need an agreement that works just as well when you want to leave the shelter as it does when you are excited about moving in. See How to Use Mexico Shelter Manufacturing to Replace Your China Manufacturing.
Your own subsidiary will usually be a sociedad anónima de capital variable (S.A. de C.V.) or a sociedad de responsabilidad limitada de capital variable (S. de R.L. de C.V.). The choice has U.S. tax consequences, because the United States treats an S.A. as a corporation, while an S. de R.L. can elect to be treated as a partnership or a disregarded entity. Your tax advisors should also look at transfer pricing and at whether your Mexican operation could create a taxable presence in Mexico for your U.S. company, which Mexico's maquiladora tax rules address directly. They should check whether you qualify for Plan México's accelerated deductions for new investment as well. Get them involved before you form anything. Changing the structure after you have begun operating can be far more troublesome than choosing the right one at the outset. See A Mexico Company Formation Guide.
Mexico's Customs Law reform, widely viewed as the most significant since 1995, took effect on January 1, 2026. It ended the protection customs brokers had when their clients supplied false or inaccurate information, so expect your broker to scrutinize you far more closely. IMMEX companies must now keep files covering not just customs records but financial flows, contracts, logistics costs, and production process records, and penalties have gone up substantially. Many foreign companies buying from China never thought about export customs compliance because their factories and freight forwarders handled it. In Mexico you will need people and systems doing this work from day one. A business that has relied on its Chinese supplier to handle virtually every customs detail needs to recognize that its responsibilities in Mexico will be considerably greater.
At least half a dozen Mexican lawyers have told us, only half joking, that American companies have far more to fear from Mexico's labor laws than from the cartels. Those laws just got more demanding. Mexico amended its Constitution on March 3, 2026, and its Federal Labor Law on May 1, 2026, to cut the maximum workweek from 48 hours to 40 with no reduction in pay.
